title: Globalization and Localization with Resource Files
description: Use .resx resource files to localize strings, validation messages, and view content across multiple cultures in ASP.NET Core.

terms.definition: Designing an application so it can support many cultures — handling input, display, and output for different languages, regions, calendars, and number formats.
Adapting a globalized application for a specific culture or locale by providing translated strings, date formats, and cultural conventions.
An XML-based file that stores culture-specific strings as key/value pairs. The file name suffix (e.g., .fr, .es) selects which culture it applies to.
A DI-injectable service that retrieves localized strings from resource files based on the current request's culture.
A service injected into Razor views to localize static text and labels within the view markup.

data.text: What Are Resource Files?

Resource files (`.resx`) are XML files that store culture-specific key/value pairs. They let you keep translated strings outside your code so translators can work without touching your C# logic. ASP.NET Core automatically picks the right resource file based on the current request's culture.

For example, if your site supports English (default), French, and Spanish, you would use three resource files for each set of strings: a base file (no suffix) for the default culture, and suffixed versions for each additional culture.

data.title: File naming convention
data.text: Resource files follow the pattern: `BaseName.[culture].resx`. For example: `JobApplication.fr.resx` for French, `JobApplication.es.resx` for Spanish. The base file `JobApplication.resx` holds the default (usually English) strings.

data.title: What each service call does
data.text: AddViewLocalization enables IViewLocalizer for Razor views. AddDataAnnotationsLocalization makes [Required], [Display], and other attribute messages pull from resource files. Configure<RequestLocalizationOptions> sets the cultures the app supports. AddLocalization sets the shared Resources folder path.
Step 2 — Enable Localization Middleware
The localization middleware must be placed **before** any middleware that reads the request culture (like routing or authorization). Add it after `app.UseRouting();` in `Program.cs`:

data.title: Program.cs — localization middleware
data.content: Pull RequestLocalizationOptions from the service container and pass it to UseRequestLocalization.

data.title: Middleware order matters
data.text: UseRequestLocalization must run before routing and authorization. If it runs after, the culture won't be set in time and resource files will fall back to the default culture.

data.text: Step 5 — Localize Strings in a Controller
Inject `IStringLocalizer<T>` into your controller to retrieve culture-specific strings. The generic type parameter tells ASP.NET Core which resource file to use.

data.title: Controllers/HomeController.cs
data.content: Inject IStringLocalizer<HomeController> to look up HomeController.{culture}.resx resource strings.

data.title: How IStringLocalizer finds the right file
data.text: When you request _localizer["Application submitted successfully"], ASP.NET Core looks for HomeController.{culture}.resx. If the key is missing from the culture-specific file, it falls back to the default resource file.
Step 6 — Localize Text in Razor Views
Use `IViewLocalizer` to translate any static text in your Razor views — headings, labels, button text, and validation summaries.

data.title: Views/Home/Index.cshtml
data.content: Inject IViewLocalizer and IOptions<RequestLocalizationOptions> to display localized strings and a culture selector.

data.text: The corresponding view resource files (`Views/Home/Index.fr.resx` and `Views/Home/Index.es.resx`) store translations for keys like `Job Application`, `Submit Application`, and `I accept the terms and conditions`.

rows: I accept the terms and conditions

data.text: Step 7 — Add a Culture Selector to the View
Let users switch cultures via a dropdown that adds `?culture=xx&ui-culture=xx` to the URL. The `QueryStringRequestCultureProvider` picks it up automatically.

data.title: Culture switcher — add to any view
data.content: A <form> with a <select> that submits the chosen culture via query string.
data.code: <form id="cultureForm" asp-action="SetLanguage" method="post" class="mb-3"> <label>@Localizer["Language"]:</label> <select name="culture" onchange="this.form.submit()" class="form-select d-inline-block w-auto ms-2"> @foreach (var item in cultureItems) { <option value="@item.Value" selected="@(item.Value == requestCulture.RequestCulture.UICulture.Name)"> @item.Text </option> } </select> </form>

data.title: Controllers/HomeController.cs — SetLanguage action
data.content: A simple POST action that sets a cookie with the chosen culture and redirects back.

data.text: Where to Place Resource Files
ASP.NET Core follows a convention-based lookup for resource files. When `ResourcesPath = "Resources"` is set, resource files are resolved from these locations:

data.title: Alternative dot-separated path
data.text: You can also use dot-separated paths: Resources/Controllers.HomeController.fr.resx, Resources/Models.JobApplication.fr.resx, and Resources/Views.Home.Index.fr.resx work the same way.

data.caption: How ASP.NET Core resolves localized strings for each request
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    A[HTTP Request with ?culture=fr] --> B[Localization Middleware]
    B --> C{QueryStringProvider}
    C -->|found| D[Set Culture = fr]
    C -->|not found| E{CookieProvider}
    E -->|found| D
    E -->|not found| F{Browser Header}
    F -->|found| D
    F -->|not found| G[Use Default en-US]
    D --> H[Controller / View renders]
    G --> H
    H --> I{IStringLocalizer lookup}
    I --> J[HomeController.fr.resx?]
    J -->|yes| K[Return French string]
    J -->|no| L[HomeController.resx fallback]
    K --> M[Rendered HTML in French]
    L --> M

data.title: Resource File vs Shared Resource File

cards.title: Per-class resource
cards.description: One .resx file per model, controller, or view. Tied to that class's name.
pros: Strings live next to their usage
cons: Harder to share common labels like 'Save' or 'Cancel'

cards.title: Shared resource file
cards.description: A single .resx file (e.g., SharedResources.resx) used across multiple classes via IStringLocalizerFactory.
cons: Less discoverable which class owns a string

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Resource files (.resx) store culture-specific key/value pairs outside your code.
Configure services with AddViewLocalization, AddDataAnnotationsLocalization, and Configure<RequestLocalizationOptions>.
UseRequestLocalization middleware must be placed before routing and authorization.
IStringLocalizer<T> is injected into controllers; IViewLocalizer is injected into Razor views.
File naming convention: BaseName.{culture}.resx — ASP.NET Core matches the file automatically.
data.takeaway: Resource files are the most widely used localization approach in ASP.NET Core. Master them first before exploring PO files.

items.question: What is the difference between Culture and UICulture?
items.answer: Culture (e.g., en-US) controls formatting of dates, numbers, and currencies. UICulture controls which resource file is loaded for translated strings. They are usually set to the same value but can be different.

items.question: Do I need a resource file for every culture?
items.answer: No. ASP.NET Core falls back to the base resource file (without a culture suffix) if a culture-specific file does not exist. The base file should always contain your default-language strings.

items.question: Can I use resource files in a class library?
items.answer: Yes. Set the ResourcesPath in AddLocalization and ensure the .resx files have their Build Action set to 'Embedded Resource'. Use IStringLocalizerFactory to create localizers for types in the library.

items.question: Why are my validation messages not translating?
items.answer: Make sure AddDataAnnotationsLocalization() is chained on AddControllersWithViews(), and that your resource file key exactly matches the ErrorMessage string in your model attribute.
